ui.tagline: Terraform on AWS with CI gates, FinOps and failure scenarios. Runs locally on an emulator: no cloud account, no cost.
ui.pipeline_intro: Every button runs the same make targets that CI runs. The apply stage waits for a manual approval, like a protected environment in GitHub Actions.
ui.approval_text: All gates passed. Review the plan log above, then approve or reject the apply.
ui.no_job: No job yet. Run the pipeline to apply the baseline.
ui.not_applied: Nothing is applied yet. Run the pipeline first.
ui.map_intro: Drawn from terraform show -json (the state), plus the live security group rules read from the emulator API.
ui.state_backend_text: S3 bucket (versioned, SSE) + DynamoDB lock table
ui.lab_intro: Each scenario injects one real fault and shows which control stops it. Plan-time faults are blocked before anything is applied; runtime faults change the emulator behind Terraform's back.
ui.compare_field_how: TODO(author): describe the method (what was timed, start and end points, how many runs).
ui.compare_lab_how: Seconds per stage, timed by the lab API around each make target. This is the emulator on your machine, not AWS: it shows where the time goes, it does not predict cloud durations.
ui.cards_intro: One card per scenario, always in the same six fields.

card.pipeline: How it works in the pipeline

ui.card_metric_live: In this lab: stopped by {control} in {s} s.
ui.card_metric_none: In this lab: not run yet (inject it in the Failure lab).
ui.card_metric_how: Seconds from injection to the failed control, timed by the lab API on the emulator.

missing-route.title: Missing route
missing-route.story: The NAT gateway is disabled to save money. The app tier silently loses its default route and its outbound access.

card.context: App subnets reach the internet only through a NAT gateway. Removing the NAT also removes their 0.0.0.0/0 route, and nothing fails until an application times out.
card.automated: A plan rule: every route table tagged Tier=public or Tier=app must have a default route; Tier=data must have none.
card.pipeline: make policy reads the plan JSON right after terraform plan and fails the run before the approval step.
card.before: Before: found after apply, by an application that cannot reach its dependencies.
card.risks: The rule depends on the Tier tag, so a route table without a valid tag fails the rule instead of being skipped.
card.validated: Applied in emulator (moto). Not executed in a real AWS account.

open-security-group.title: Open security group
open-security-group.story: A temporary rule opens the database port to 0.0.0.0/0 so someone can debug from home.

card.context: The database security group should accept connections from the app tier only. A wide-open rule is the classic shortcut that never gets removed.
card.automated: A custom Checkov policy (CKV2_LAB_1) rejects any security group ingress from 0.0.0.0/0, on top of the built-in checks.
card.pipeline: make scan runs Checkov on the resolved plan, so the value is checked even when it arrives through a variable.
card.before: Before: depends on a reviewer noticing one CIDR in a diff.
card.risks: Skipped checks are listed in .checkov.yaml, each with its reason. A new skip is visible in code review.
card.validated: Scan executed locally on the plan. Not executed in a real AWS account.

costly-resource.title: Forgotten costly resource
costly-resource.story: A load test sized the database up to db.r6g.xlarge Multi-AZ and nobody sized it back down.

card.context: Instance class and Multi-AZ are one-line changes that multiply the bill. They pass every functional test.
card.automated: An offline estimate per resource from the plan, compared with a monthly budget. In CI, Infracost can replace the reference price table.
card.pipeline: make cost prints the estimate and fails when the total is over BUDGET (100 USD/month in the lab).
card.before: Before: found on the invoice, weeks later.
card.risks: Prices are a labelled reference snapshot (finops/prices.json), not a quote. Unknown instance classes are flagged, never priced as zero. Data transfer is not estimated.
card.validated: Estimate executed locally on the plan with reference list prices. Infracost was not run.

state-lock.title: Stale state lock
state-lock.story: A pipeline job is cancelled in the middle of an apply and never releases its lock. Every later run is blocked.

card.context: The DynamoDB lock prevents two runs from writing the same state. A killed job leaves the lock behind.
card.automated: Every plan and apply uses the remote backend with locking and -lock-timeout=0s, so a held lock fails fast with the lock ID and owner.
card.pipeline: The plan stage fails with 'Error acquiring the state lock'. After confirming the owner is dead, make unlock ID=<id> releases it.
card.before: Before (local state, no lock): two concurrent applies can corrupt the state.
card.risks: force-unlock on a lock that is still alive causes exactly the corruption the lock prevents: confirm the owner first. The lab simulates the killed job by writing the lock item directly.
card.validated: Applied in emulator (moto S3 + DynamoDB). Not executed in a real AWS account.

drift.title: Drift
drift.story: Someone adds an ingress rule to the database security group by hand, outside Terraform.

card.context: Manual changes make the real infrastructure differ from the code. The next apply may revert them, or worse, they stay unnoticed.
card.automated: terraform plan -detailed-exitcode as a drift check. Security group rules are inline, so Terraform owns the whole rule set and sees rules it did not create.
card.pipeline: make drift fails with DRIFT DETECTED and shows the diff. The fix is a normal plan + apply, which removes the manual rule.
card.before: Before: the rule is found in an audit, or never.
card.risks: Only attributes Terraform manages are compared. With standalone rule resources, a rule added by hand would not be detected.
card.validated: Applied in emulator (moto). Not executed in a real AWS account.

dirty-destroy.title: Dirty destroy
dirty-destroy.story: A security group and a network interface are created by hand inside the VPC. They are not in the state.

card.context: On AWS, resources created outside Terraform block the VPC deletion with DependencyViolation, or survive the destroy and keep costing money.
card.automated: orphan-check lists everything in the account that is not in the Terraform state, and whether it carries the ManagedBy tag.
card.pipeline: make orphan-check runs after every destroy and fails when anything is left. It can also run on a schedule.
card.before: Before: leftovers are found by reading the console region by region.
card.risks: The check covers the resource types this lab creates, not every AWS service. The emulator does not enforce DependencyViolation, so the lab shows the detection, not the failed destroy.
card.validated: Applied in emulator (moto). Not executed in a real AWS account.

secret-leak.title: Secret leak
secret-leak.story: A deploy.env file with an AWS access key is about to be committed.

card.context: A key pushed to a repository must be treated as compromised, even if the commit is removed later.
card.automated: gitleaks scans the working tree in the pipeline. The lab generates a random fake key at runtime, so the repository never contains one.
card.pipeline: make secrets fails with 'leaks found' and the file and line, with the value redacted.
card.before: Before: the key is found by whoever scans public repositories first.
card.risks: Detection is pattern-based: unusual secret formats need custom rules. Removing the file is not enough, the key must be revoked.
card.validated: Scan executed locally. The pipeline uses OIDC roles in the documented cloud setup, so no long-lived key exists to leak.

RDS instance, subnet group, security group
API mock: no database engine runs
RDS parameter group values (rds.force_ssl) and Performance Insights
The emulator does not keep them
Alarms never fire: the emulator has no metrics
Remote state in S3 (versioning, SSE) with DynamoDB lock
TLS-only bucket policy on the state bucket
Checkov, route and tag policy, cost gate, gitleaks
Run on the plan inside the lab container
Azure modules: VNet with NSGs and NAT gateway, Monitor alerts
terraform validate + Checkov only: no account, never planned or applied
Kubernetes demonstration manifests (deployment, network policies, autoscaler)
Checkov only: not applied to any cluster, not EKS or AKS
Bundled terraform ruleset, verified in the CI run
Needs an API key; the lab uses the offline price table
GitHub Actions: ci workflow (gates and end-to-end tests)
GitHub Actions: apply and destroy workflows
Anything in a real AWS account
Nothing was executed in a real account
adrs: LocalStack now requires an account and auth token. moto is open source, needs no account and covers every service used here.
Newer provider versions (6.40 and 6.73 were tested) use a CloudWatch wire protocol that moto 5.2.5 does not answer. 6.20.0 is the newest version verified to work.
Gates run on the plan JSON, not on raw HCL
Variables are already resolved in the plan, so a bad value passed by tfvars is caught. One file feeds Checkov, the policy and the cost gate.
One Makefile for people, CI and the UI
What the UI shows is exactly what CI runs. There is no second implementation to drift.
Routes as separate resources, security group rules inline
A removed inline route block is ignored by the provider. Inline security group rules give Terraform exclusive ownership, which is what detects manual rules.

Terraform now prefers use_lockfile (native S3 locking). The table is kept because many existing estates still use it and it makes the stale-lock scenario visible. Migration is a one-line backend change.
A filesystem mirror in the image means make up needs no registry access at runtime, and the provider version cannot float.
UI in plain HTML and JavaScript, docs inside the UI
No build step, no CDN, works offline. Easy to read from top to bottom.
lessons: A TLS-only bucket policy locks an HTTP emulator out of its own state bucket. The policy is validated by plan and scan only.
Deleting an inline route block does not delete the route. The first version of the missing-route scenario passed the gate for that reason.
The emulator drops RDS parameter values and Performance Insights, which shows as permanent drift. The lab passes none there and keeps the secure defaults for real accounts.
Creating the RDS instance takes about 80 seconds even on the emulator, because the provider waits and polls. Measured on this lab.
Checkov tries to download guidelines on every run. --skip-download keeps it offline.
After a destroy the emulator keeps the NAT gateway's network interface in a VPC that no longer exists. orphan-check ignores interfaces without a VPC and documents why.
The dependency lock file is not committed: hashes for every platform cannot be generated offline. The provider version is pinned exactly instead.
Cost: the lab costs nothing. By the reference list prices, the baseline would cost about 55 USD/month on AWS, and the NAT gateway is the largest line.

migration.title: On-premises to cloud migration runbook
migration.note: A written procedure for moving an application and its PostgreSQL database into the network built by these modules. It has not been executed: the emulator runs no database engine, so there is nothing to restore into.
steps: 1. Inventory
List servers, databases, versions, sizes, scheduled jobs, certificates and who owns each one.
Every item has an owner and a target (move, replace or retire).
2. Dependencies
Map who calls whom: ports, DNS names, fixed IPs, file shares, outbound integrations.
Each flow is a rule you can write in a security group, and nothing depends on an IP that will change.
3. Strategy
Choose per component: rehost (same thing on a VM), replatform (database to RDS) or refactor. Default to the smallest change that removes the on-premises dependency.
The choice and its reason are written down for every component.
4. Landing zone
Create network, database and monitoring with the pipeline, in a non-production environment first. Connect on-premises through VPN or Direct Connect.
Pipeline is green, the route and security group gates pass, and a test host on-premises reaches the database port.
5. Data copy
Initial load with pg_dump and pg_restore, or AWS DMS with change data capture when the allowed downtime is short. Rehearse at least once with production-sized data.
Row counts and checksums match, and the rehearsal time fits inside the window.
6. Cutover
Lower the DNS TTL days before. In the window: stop writes, let replication catch up, switch the connection string or DNS, start the application.
The application serves traffic from the cloud and the alarms stay quiet.
7. Validation
Run smoke tests and business checks, compare error rate and latency with the baseline, confirm backups and alarms are active.
The owner signs off inside the window.
8. Rollback
Decide before the window what triggers a rollback and until when it is possible. Keep the old database read-only and untouched until the decision point passes.
Either the sign-off is given or DNS points back, with no data written on only one side.

overview: A Terraform lab for AWS with the controls a production pipeline needs: quality and security gates before the plan is approved, a cost budget, drift and orphan detection, and seven failure scenarios that prove each control works. Everything runs on a local AWS emulator, so there is no cloud account and no cost.

git clone <this repository> && cd <folder>
make up        # builds the image, starts the emulator, opens http://localhost:8080
make ci        # every gate, in pipeline order
make test      # apply, inject the seven failures, destroy, orphan-check
make down      # stop and wipe everything
The only thing installed on the machine.
Optional. Without it: docker compose up -d --build --wait
Downloads the base image, Terraform, the providers and the gate tools. Nothing is downloaded at runtime.
Runs the gates, waits for a manual approval, applies. Each stage has its status, duration and log.
The applied topology, read from the Terraform state, with the live security group rules.
Inject each fault and watch the control that stops it.
Stage durations measured in this lab.
Each scenario in six fixed fields.
Estimated monthly cost, tag policy and resources outside the state.
architecture: Two containers. The emulator answers the AWS API in memory. The lab container holds Terraform, the providers, the gate tools, the API and this UI. The UI never runs Terraform itself: it asks the API, and the API runs the same make targets that CI runs.
In-memory AWS API: S3, DynamoDB, EC2/VPC, RDS, CloudWatch, IAM, Logs.
Runs make targets as jobs, one at a time, and records each stage. Reads the state for the map and FinOps views.
No build step and no external request. English and Portuguese.
One implementation used by people, CI and the UI.
Starts the same containers and runs make ci and make test.
Flow of one pipeline run: fmt, validate, tflint, gitleaks, plan, Checkov on the plan, route and tag policy, cost budget, manual approval, apply. Any failed gate stops the run before the approval.
The environment applied on the emulator.
Reference wiring of the Azure modules.
Input files of the plan-time failure scenarios.
Plan policy, cost estimate, orphan check.
modules: Every module has typed variables with validation, outputs, and exact provider versions. Standard tags (Project, Env, Owner, CostCenter, ManagedBy) come from the provider default_tags, so no resource can forget them.
VPC, three subnet tiers per AZ (public, app, data), internet gateway, optional NAT gateway, one route table per tier, locked default security group, flow logs to CloudWatch.
enable_nat_gateway (cost), single_nat_gateway (cheaper, no AZ redundancy), azs (2 to 4).
PostgreSQL instance in the data tier, subnet group, security group with inline rules, parameter group forcing TLS, master password managed by Secrets Manager, encryption, backups, IAM authentication.
allowed_cidr_blocks (least privilege), instance_class and multi_az (cost), deletion_protection.
Application log group with retention, three RDS alarms (CPU, connections, free storage), dashboard, optional SNS topic.
Subnet layout: the VPC is a /16 and each subnet is a /20. Each tier owns a block of four indexes, so adding an AZ never renumbers an existing subnet.
Public tier: default route to the internet gateway.
App tier: default route to the NAT gateway. Without NAT it has no outbound access, and the route policy fails the plan.
Data tier: no default route at all. The policy fails the plan if one appears.
state: The state lives in S3 and is locked through DynamoDB. bootstrap/ creates both once, with local state; every other root module then uses the remote backend.
A bad state write can be rolled back to the previous version.
The state contains resource attributes that should not be readable at rest.
The bucket can never be exposed by a wrong ACL or policy.
Requests over plain HTTP are denied. Validated by plan and scan only: the emulator speaks HTTP.
Two runs cannot write the same state. A second run fails fast with the lock ID.
Moving an existing local state to the backend: add the backend block, run terraform init -migrate-state, confirm, then delete the local file. The lab starts directly on the remote backend.
Terraform now prefers native S3 locking (use_lockfile) and marks dynamodb_table as deprecated. The table is kept here on purpose; see Decisions.
pipeline: Gates run on the plan exported as JSON, so every variable is already resolved. A bad value passed by a tfvars file is caught exactly like a bad value written in the module.
Syntax and type errors, in the AWS and Azure environments.
Deprecated syntax, unused declarations, missing types.
Anything the provider rejects; also fails fast on a held state lock.
Insecure settings, plus the custom rule against 0.0.0.0/0 ingress.
Insecure settings in the Azure modules and Kubernetes manifests.
A tier without its default route, an isolated tier with one, a resource without the standard tags.
Nothing is applied without it. In GitHub Actions this is a protected environment.
Applies exactly the plan file that passed the gates.
Fails when real infrastructure differs from the code.
Lists anything that exists but is not in the state.
Plans a failure scenario by hand.
Real account: the workflows document the change in a comment. Replace the emulator with an OIDC role (aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials), so the pipeline holds no long-lived key.
scenarios: Each scenario injects one fault and names the control that must stop it. A test fails if the fault is caught by a different control, or not at all. Run them in the Failure lab tab; the Scenario cards tab explains each one.
Plan-time faults only change input variables. They are blocked before anything is applied.
Runtime faults change the emulator directly through its API, the way a person with console access would.
The secret is a random fake key generated when you click. The repository never contains one.
finops: Three controls keep cost visible before the invoice arrives.
An estimate per resource from the plan, compared with a monthly budget (BUDGET, 100 USD in the lab). The run fails when the total is above it.
Every taggable resource must carry Project, Env, Owner, CostCenter and ManagedBy. Checked on the plan.
Anything that exists outside the state is listed, with a note when it has no ManagedBy tag.

Prices in finops/prices.json are reference on-demand list prices for us-east-1, a labelled snapshot and not a quote. Data transfer, log ingestion and Secrets Manager are not estimated. An instance class missing from the table is reported as unknown, never as zero.

Variables marked COST in their description are the ones that move the bill: NAT gateway, instance class, Multi-AZ, log retention. Infracost can replace the price table in CI when the repository has an INFRACOST_API_KEY secret.
azure: The Azure modules mirror the AWS network and monitoring modules. They are checked with terraform validate and Checkov only. There is no Azure account or emulator behind the lab, so they have never been planned or applied.
Virtual network, one subnet per tier, one NSG per tier, database port open from the app tier only, default outbound access disabled on private tiers, optional NAT gateway.
Log Analytics workspace, three metric alerts for a PostgreSQL Flexible Server, optional action group.
kubernetes: k8s/demo-app.yaml is a stateless web workload written the way it would go to EKS or AKS. It is checked by Checkov in the pipeline and has not been applied to any cluster.
No root, no privilege escalation, read-only filesystem
Image cannot change under the same name
CPU and memory requests and limits.
Survives the loss of one zone
Two replicas with a zone spread constraint.
A default-deny NetworkPolicy, then one policy allowing HTTP to the pods.
PodDisruptionBudget with one pod always available.
HorizontalPodAutoscaler from 2 to 6 replicas at 70% CPU.
No API credentials in the pod
troubleshooting: Another process uses the port. Stop it, or change the published port in docker-compose.yml.
The lab is creating the state backend. Check make logs; the emulator must be reachable at http://moto:5000 inside the network.
A previous run was interrupted. Read the lock ID in the message and run make unlock ID=<id>, after making sure no run is alive.
A button answers 'another job is running'
Jobs share one Terraform state and run one at a time. Wait for the current job.
